extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature interested in James Joyce's Ulysses
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the evaluative and descriptive criteria found in the Wikipedia article for assessing James Joyce's Ulysses — its techniques, structure, themes, and reception. Useful for readers or students analyzing what qualities critics and scholars highlight as important about the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Ulysses' stream of consciousness technique — foregrounding the process of thinking and rendering internal thought flows directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Joyce 'foregrounded the process of thinking' and that before Joyce 'no writer of fiction had so foregrounded the process of thinking.' This technique changes focus wildly (see Episode 3 'Proteus') and is central to judgments about the novel's psychological realism and difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful structuring / Homeric correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful structuring that establishes parallels between Ulysses' 18 episodes and Homer's Odyssey (tripartite division, mapping episodes to Homeric episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes Gilbert and Linati schemata that make links to the Odyssey clear; Joyce referred to episodes by their Homeric titles. Critics view this structural mapping as a scaffold or means of construction — a central criterion for analyses of the book's form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental prose (puns, parodies, epiphanies, allusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose of an experimental nature — 'replete with puns, parodies, epiphanies and allusions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cluster of techniques is cited as a defining quality. Examples include dense parody in Episode 14 and varied registers throughout; evaluators look for inventive language play and novelistic experiments when assessing the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rich characterisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich, full-bodied characterisation of principal figures (Leopold Bloom, Molly Bloom, Stephen Dedalus) and their psychological interiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes the novel's close attention to characters' inner lives across a single day. The depth and complexity of characterization is frequently cited as a measure of the novel's achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: High degree of allusiveness / intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly allusive text with references and correspondences to works/figures such as Homer, Shakespeare, Dante, Jesus, Elijah, Moses, Don Juan and many others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel's meaning and richness depend on recognition of intertexts; critics note its many literary, religious and mythological allusions. Assessing the novel often involves mapping these allusions and their function in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of styles / episodic stylistic variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Written in a variety of styles across its 18 episodes, including shifts in narrative voice and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual episodes employ distinct modes (e.g., Episode 15 as a play script, Episode 17 as a mathematical catechism, Episode 18 as unpunctuated monologue). Evaluations consider how successfully Joyce sustains or uses this stylistic plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody and pastiche
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive parody and pastiche of other authors, registers and historical styles (e.g., parodies of Malory, the King James Bible, Bunyan, Dickens, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episode 14 famously recapitulates English-language history through parodic registers. Critics assess the skill and purpose of such parodies — whether they illuminate themes or become merely virtuoso display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay and linguistic experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensive wordplay, linguistic inventiveness and experimentation (puns, latinate prose, Anglo-Saxon alliteration, recapitulation of English language history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights Joyce's technical virtuosity (e.g., Episode 14's language-history sequence). Evaluators look at dexterity with register, etymology, and phonetic/semantic play as a core merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time and compressed temporal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative takes place over a single day (16–17 June 1904), producing temporal unity and intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-day frame is central to the novel's design and affects judgments about pacing, detail, and the representation of ordinary life magnified into epic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed geographic realism / local Dublin mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise depiction of Dublin locations and movements (map of route, detailed settings like 7 Eccles Street, Davy Byrne's pub, National Library, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel's grounding in real places anchors its experimental techniques; critics often examine how local detail interacts with mythic parallels and character trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic engagement with social, political and religious issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit engagement with themes such as antisemitism, human sexuality, British rule in Ireland, Catholicism and Irish nationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames these themes as treated in the context of early-20th-century Dublin; assessments consider the novel's moral/social commentary and its historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal experimentation across narrative modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multiple formal modes (play script, catechism Q&A, newspaper headlines, vignettes) rather than a single conventional narrative voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each episode's form is a formal experiment; critics judge the coherence and artistic justification of these shifts and the ways they reflect characters' minds or thematic concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty, obscurity and dense reference network
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is 'not an easy book to read or to understand' — episodes contain obscure references and foreign phrases that contribute to perceived difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics note the novel's opacity; guidance cited (judge in obscenity ruling) recommends reading secondary works/schemata. Difficulty is a feature and a barrier; evaluation often factors in accessibility vs. richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frank depiction of sexuality and bodily functions (controversial content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit sexual content and bodily detail (e.g., masturbation, defecation) which historically led to obscenity prosecutions and censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments must balance claims about realism, artistic purpose, and social offense; the book's frankness is central to both praise and criticism and has legal/cultural implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour and comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad humour and comic treatment (vis comica) interwoven with experimental techniques and character portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour is cited as one of the elements that contribute to the novel's achievement; critics evaluate its effectiveness in balancing experiment and human feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural layering and multiple mythic/religious frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative composed of multiple levels (Homeric pattern, Christian pattern, present/particular personal level) producing layered meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William York Tindall and others describe the novel as a composition of several levels; evaluations look at how these frameworks interrelate and whether mythic overlays enhance or overwhelm the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation and literary influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of originality and the work's influence on the novel form — claims that Ulysses 'set the standard of the novel so high' and was 'a demonstration and summation' of modernism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics judge Ulysses partly by its historical impact and its success in redefining possibilities for fiction (technical innovations, scale, and ambition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of over-systematisation / excessive symbolism (potential pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms that Joyce's 'taste for symbolism' or systematisation can 'overrun the bounds of art into an arid ingenuity' that substitutes puzzle for organic narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edmund Wilson's critique is cited as an anti-pattern: when symbolic scaffolding takes precedence over narrative truthfulness, the result may seem artificial. Evaluations may weigh symbolic density against naturalistic demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial recording of simultaneous perception/speech/thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Joyce's method of 'recorded, simultaneously, what a man says, sees, thinks' — the attempt to render speech, perception and thought together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal/technique criterion: assessors consider how effectively the prose integrates external action, spoken language and internal monologue without privileging one register unduly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epiphanies
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of 'epiphanies' as an element of the novel's technique and meaning-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epiphanic moments (sudden insights or revelations) are a stylistic and thematic device. Critics evaluate their placement, frequency, and contribution to character understanding and thematic resolution.
